title: Decide first, then regenerate once
statement: Settle the decisions that change what content must be, such as its target level, before regenerating anything, then fold every fix into one gated regeneration.
example: One remediation plan refused to regenerate 75 passages before deciding whether the course was meant to be at grade level, and the decision it recorded needed no passage rebuild.
detail: A grade-6 reading course's remediation plan, written after an adversarial review, ordered its work by dependency and leverage rather than severity: two critical findings were decisions, not builds, and they gated the costly content work (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-REMEDIATION-SEQUENCE.md`, lines 4-6). Because raising the reading level forces passage regeneration and the items are tied to their passages, it folded every content fix into one gated regeneration rather than re-shipping the items five times (lines 39-41). The decision recorded afterwards, following a recheck of the reading-level estimate, found the texts already at band, so the build needed no passage rebuild (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g6-reading/G6-FORK-DECISION.md`, lines 14 and 16).
against: It rests on one plan, and the five-fold re-ship it avoided is the plan's own projection, not a measured cost.

evidence.quote: **Ordering principle:** dependencies + leverage, not raw severity. Two Criticals are *decisions*, not builds, and they gate the expensive content work. Do not regenerate 75 passages before deciding whether the course is even meant to be at grade level.
